Morpheus's three-branch memory graph is motivated by two foundational theories from cognitive science: Tulving's memory classification (1972) distinguishes episodic memory (personal events situated in time and place) from semantic memory (general knowledge detached from specific episodes). Morpheus adds a third branch — procedural — following the broader taxonomy that includes "knowing how" alongside "knowing what" and "remembering when." Complementary Learning Systems theory (McClelland, McNaughton & O'Reilly, 1995) argues that effective memory requires two complementary systems: a fast-learning system that captures specific episodes, and a slow-learning system that gradually extracts structure. In Morpheus, the episodic branch captures events as they occur (one fact per node, organized by date), while the semantic branch consolidates facts and relationships across conversations over time. Cross-branch LINK edges (involves, instance_of, learned_from) serve as the binding mechanism between the two systems. Root├── Semantic — facts, entities, relationships (by topic)├── Episodic — events and activities (by date)└── Procedural — workflows and procedures (by domain) Ingestion: Opus 4.7 (max effort), one session at a time, one fact per leaf. Episodic events as flat siblings under dates, chained with continues links. Procedural concepts auto-spawn Pitfalls children. Retrieval (Fly Swatter Search): 5 FTS5 + 5 vector results, plus top 20 neighborhood nodes ranked by embedding similarity. get-node provides query-ranked neighbors and ±14-day episodic windows.

Full LOCOMO suite (10 of 10 conversations, 1977 questions). Different judge model — Claude Opus 4.7 vs gpt-4.1-mini for other systems. One-pass ingestion — multi-pass reinforcement would improve cross-concept linking and single-hop completeness. Image-dependent questions — some details require visual recognition.

These results are from a single ingestion pass — each session processed once, graph never revisited. In practice, important concepts are reinforced across recurring conversations. We expect single-hop to improve as cross-concept links are established through topic recurrence.

Rescue group Count % of 183 Adversarial — handled correctly 49 27% Hedged but correct 45 25% Benchmark error / source contradiction 31 17% Multiple valid answers 24 13% Latent-knowledge required (prompt-compliant abstain) 20 11% Synonyms / equivalent phrasing 8 4% Commitment-layer convention disagreement 6 3% What this says about the benchmark-vs-system mismatch. Across the 183 rescues, four classes dominate: LLM-judge limitations (102 of 183, 56%) — string-match misses on adversarial structure (27%), semantic equivalence (hedged 25% + synonyms 4% = 29%). Better judging would catch these. Benchmark flaws (31 of 183, 17%) — date typos, subject misattributions, category errors (sushi-as-drink), expected facts not in source (e.g., conv-49 Q104's "spinach/avocado/strawberries bowl" not in source, conv-50 Q19's "car museum" not in source), source-thin items (conv-50 Q61 Mustang work-duration inference requires linking events the source does not connect). Independent of the judge. Test-design mismatch (26 of 183, 14%) — questions where the expected answer requires latent LLM knowledge (20, including clinical/demographic inference cases that AI agents should refuse), where two valid English interpretations diverge (6 commitment-layer convention). Per the retrieval prompt's "Answer only from what you find in the graph" directive, the agent's behavior is correct on these. Genuine rater disagreement (24 of 183, 13%) — multiple-valid open-domain inferences where reasonable raters could pick different answers. Conv-50 added 6 (post-tour excitement, Calvin-August city, workshop duration, October-weekend activity, Dave's car-origin story, Dave's recent art). The implication: the rescored numbers are a more honest measure of memory quality, and the gap between raw and rescored is itself a useful signal — a system whose raw is far below its rescored is producing right-but-hedged answers, correctly handling adversarial swaps, or principled abstaining on out-of-scope latent-knowledge questions; a system whose raw and rescored are equal is either producing literal-match answers, lacks adversarial handling, or is silently using LLM world knowledge to fill gaps the graph didn't capture.

To test this fairly we have to normalize by session size — longer sessions naturally consume more tokens regardless of where they sit in the conversation. Dividing each session's total tokens by its turn count gives a per-unit-content rate: And averaged across conversations with min-max envelope: Linear fit (sessions 2+, omitting session 1 cold-start)​ To check whether the post-cold-start cost has any trend with session position, we fit a linear model to all 262 sessions with session_num ≥ 2, treating each session as a sample from the per-session-position distribution: Results: Parameter Value Intercept 604.8 ± 32.4 K tokens / turn Slope 0.27 ± 1.90 K tokens / turn per session R² 0.0001 t-statistic on slope 0.14 n 262 sessions (across 10 conversations) The slope is statistically indistinguishable from zero (t = 0.14, far below the t > 2 threshold for 95% significance). The 95% confidence interval on the slope is [−3.5, +4.0] K tokens/turn per session — the data is consistent with a perfectly flat plateau, OR with a tiny drift in either direction. The added 30 conv-50 sessions tightened the confidence interval and pushed the t-statistic even closer to zero. Findings — hypothesis confirmed​ Cold-start is dramatic. Session 1 averages 159 K tokens / turn (n=10) vs sessions 2+ averaging 609 K tokens / turn. A ~4× cold-start gap — with an empty graph, the agent has nothing to cross-reference and extracts each fact independently. Post-cold-start, the cost per turn is genuinely flat. Bucketed averages stay in the 438-680 K range with no monotonic trend: Session range n Mean K tokens / turn 1 (cold start) 10 159 2-5 40 663 6-10 50 664 11-15 50 438 16-20 48 619 21-25 40 678 26-32 34 619 The variance across session positions (438-678) is smaller than the within-position variance (stdev ~165-285) at any given session number. There's no signal in the position dimension — only noise from session-level content differences. Cache_read drives the plateau. Cache_read dominates ingest tokens (~85%). As the graph grows, neighborhood-expansion queries return larger context — but the agent's per-turn working set is bounded by what it actually needs to retrieve to extract the current session, not by graph total size. Graph growth is sublinear in session count once the major entities are established, so cache_read per turn stabilizes at the agent's typical query depth. The takeaway​ The hypothesis is strongly confirmed: post-cold-start, ingest cost per turn is flat at ~605 K, with no statistically detectable trend over 30+ sessions. The cold-start gap is the single largest factor — once the agent has any graph to reference, per-turn cost stabilizes at ~4× the cold-start rate and stays there. Practical consequence: ingest cost per conversation scales as (one cold-start session) + (linear in total turn count). For a 30-session conversation with ~19 turns/session like Calvin & Dave, that's ~6 M (cold start) + ~29 × 19 × 605 K ≈ ~340 M tokens — within 8% of the observed 315 M total.

documents.t: Phase Tokens Cost Ingest (272 sessions) 3.39 B $16,140 Retrieval (1,977 questions, measured) 224 M $1,097 Total 3.61 B ~$17,240 The entire 10-conversation LOCOMO suite — graph generation + answering all 1,977 benchmark questions — costs roughly the price of a mid-tier laptop. Per question, that's $8.72 fully-loaded (ingest + retrieval), or $0.555 marginal if the graph already exists.

Cost calculations use Opus 4 standard-tier prices: input $15/MTok, cache write 5m $18.75/MTok, cache read $1.50/MTok, output $75/MTok. Retrieval costs reported here are from the original benchmark runs mined from the ~/.claude/projects/ archive. These are not re-runs and reflect actual benchmark execution cost. Ingest used effort=max Opus 4.7 with one-pass extraction. A multi-pass refinement run would substantially increase ingest cost but might improve cross-concept linking and reduce the list-completeness misses observed in the Error Analysis. The 5-min ephemeral cache window matters — running questions in tight succession amortizes cache creation across more turns. The original benchmark ran sequentially per conversation, so the cache hit rate within a conversation is high but new conversations pay full cache-create cost on the first few questions.
